The House resumed from Monday, June 7, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mazankowski that Bill C-129, an Act to provide for the continuance of Air Canada under the Canada Business Corporations Act and for the issuance and sale of shares thereof to the public, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee; and the motion of Mr. McDermid:
That this question be now put.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure and an honour to rise in my place today to speak in support of Bill C-129, a Bill which will give Canadians an opportunity to share in the future of Air Canada.
This legislation has been welcomed by Canadians from across the country-by consumers, Air Canada employees, the airline industry, not to mention the Canadian public at large. The Canadian public has welcomed it because it means increased competition. Increased competition means better service for consumers. Air Canada employees have welcomed it because it means expanded opportunities for the company in the future, and an opportunity for them to share in the growth of their labours.
This legislation is fully consistent with the competitive environment created by the National Transportation Act, which Act was passed just last year. That Act replaced a 20-year old law and revamped the transportation sector. It permits greater reliance on market forces and less reliance on economic regulation. The results of this are beginning to be felt in more innovation and enterprise, as well as more competitive transportation services with reduced prices.
For the airlines this has meant that it will be much easier to adjust their services to meet the demands of the market-place and to tailor their fare structure to meet competitive conditions.
The short title of Bill C-129 is the Air Canada Public Participation Act. This is an apt description of what this legislation is all about.
The intent of the Bill is to provide all Canadians with the unique opportunity to become real and active partners in the ownership of one of the world's great airlines. Once the Bill is passed, Air Canada's 22,000 plus employees, all of whom have contributed to the airline's national and international success and achievements, will also be able to share directly in the company's ownership and success.
I would remind Hon. Members as well that the legislation before us limits the level of individual ownership and, in so doing, broadens the base of potential investors.
June 7, 1988

The Air Canada Public Participation Act will ensure that no more than 10 per cent of Air Canada can ever be owned or controlled by an individual or any associated interests. There need be no concern about Canadians ever losing control of Air Canada. The legislation parallels the National Transportation Act, 1987 in that regard by restricting non-resident ownership to no more than 25 per cent of publicly available voting shares.
Air Canada, I repeat, will remain Canadian-owned and controlled. The only difference will be that Canadians, including the airline's employees, will be able to share directly in a Canadian enterprise that has become a symbol of excellence world-wide.
Most things will not change. It will be business as usual. Air Canada will be continuing its current employment and safety practices and polices, after public participation. Legislation such as the Canada Labour Code, the National Transportation Act, the Pension Benefits Standards Act and the Aeronautics Act will still apply to Air Canada, regardless of its ownership status.
The Government's commitment to maintaining a high level of safety in the Canadian transportation system will not be jeopardized. Safety has not been deregulated, and will likewise not be affected by public participation. This Government believes in regulating "smarter", and in some cases that means less regulation, in other cases more, but in all cases it means better regulation.
The Air Canada Public Participation Act will guarantee the continuance of the airline's operational and overhaul centres in Winnipeg, Mississauga and Montreal. Its head office will remain in Montreal.
In addition, the Official Languages Act continues to apply to Air Canada, thus ensuring service in both official languages.
When the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) spoke during this debate, he referred to the support this legislation has elicited from all across the country and from all sectors and interests. They welcome it because they want to see Air Canada maintain its position of respect among the world's airlines. They welcome public participation because they know that a flexible, unfettered Air Canada will continue to prosper in the new environment that has resulted from the economic regulatory reform of the Canadian airline industry.
The Government's program of economic regulatory reform has meant that more people have been able to fly to more places at better prices than ever before. It means that Canadians have benefited from increased innovation, initiative, entrepreneurial spirit and competition in the air industry. Canada's airline industry has one of the world's best airline safety records.
Transport Canada's essential role will continue to be the regulatory and enforcement body of airline safety in the testing and licencing of flight and maintenance personnel and
Air Canada
the regulations regarding aircraft maintenance and operations including inspections. Air Canada and all other Canadian airlines must comply with these regulations irrespective of ownership, as is the case today. In the context of airline safety records, it seems very appropriate that it is the Hon. Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) who has introduced this legislation. Members of this House will recall that in his former capacity as Transport Minister in 1979 he set in motion the reform of air safety standards in this country through the study undertaken by Mr. Justice Dubin. The Dubin report was the long overdue examination of air safety. Its recommendations were wide-ranging and comprehensive. They addressed air worthiness, accident and incident reporting, enforcement, navigational aids, uncontrolled airports and personnel.
For example, one of the key recommendations contained in the Dubin report called for the establishment of an independent Aviation Safety Board. This board became fully operational in October, 1984. Its objective is to advance aviation safety by conducting independent investigations into aviation occurrences, identifying safety deficiencies and making recommendations to eliminate or reduce those deficiencies.
The Canadian Aviation Safety Board accident investigation lab here in Ottawa is one of the most sophisticated facilities of its kind in the world. It is there that specialized laboratory testing and analysis of aircraft parts, structural components and wreckage from aviation occurrences is conducted. The engineering function also includes wreckage search and recovery, such as the recent recovery of literally thousands of pieces of aircraft wreckage from the bottom of Hamilton harbour. I think we can all agree, Mr. Speaker, that these are not pleasant tasks but they are essential to ensuring the continued provision of safe air transportation.
Another Dubin recommendation that has since been implemented is the creation of the Civil Aviation Tribunal to hear and determine appeals from administrative decisions quickly and fairly. This tribunal is unique in the world and permits carriers or individuals to seek an independent review if, for example, they object to the imposition of a fine.
Finally, a discussion of the Dubin recommendations is not complete until we also address the amendments to the Aeronautics Act as amended in 1985. These amendments reflected a number of the Dubin recommendations and gave this country one of the most progressive aviation safety laws in existence. The Aeronautics Act, 1985, modernized and replaced safety legislation that had not been amended in any significant way since World War II. The amended legislation has strengthened the areas of airport security, government access to pilots and engineers' records, owner and operator insurance requirements, standards for air worthiness, air traffic services and navigational aids and medical check-ups for those holding licences. Most important, Transport Canada's enforcement powers have been increased and penalties for infractions have been strengthened. This involved amending the Criminal Code as well so that some aviation

June 7, 1988
Air Canada
safety infractions are now considered criminal rather than civil offences.
As a means of properly administering the new Aeronautics Act, Transport Canada has undertaken an assessment of how best to employ in its certification, surveillance, monitoring and enforcement resources. But these new safety measures do not stop with the Aeronautics Act, Mr. Speaker.
Since 1985, Transport Canada has directed an additional $70 million toward enhancements to security at Canada's airports. This includes better physical security, more security guards and a better security inspection program. Among the further measures aimed at making air travel safe for all Canadians is the Canadian air space systems plan. This program is part of the Government's continuing commitment to develop world class technology in this country. The air space systems plan helps Transport Canada to keep pace with the rapid technological improvements in aviation safety. One aspect of this plan that is well under way is the radar modernization project. At a total estimated cost of $810 million, approximately half of which has already been spent, this initiative will improve air traffic control across the country. The bottom line is increased safety for Canada's air travellers. This was all accomplished long before initiatives such as regulatory reform and now public participation of Air Canada. Canada is the only country in the world that undertook a comprehensive review of our air safety regulations before pursuing economic regulatory reform initiatives.
Indeed, these accomplishments in the area of transportation safety made regulatory reform possible. Today it is not necessary to regulate how much a carrier can charge for a fare. What really matters is whether that carrier can operate safely. Likewise, it is not necessary for the Government to own Air Canada to ensure that it will continue to operate safely. For two years now improved regulations have been in place to ensure the safe operation for every carrier in the airline industry, including Air Canada. The Government has no difficulty with the question of where to spend taxpayers' hard earned money. We believe in using tax dollars where they will best benefit the people of Canada as a whole.
An Air Canada with access to equity markets will be willing and able to purchase aircraft on its own. The people of Canada are eager to participate by investing their capital in the future of a well-run airline. We believe that government dollars are better spent regulating air safety. This is where tax money should be going rather than buying an aircraft for an airline that would prefer having the freedom to buy them on its own and without someone looking over its shoulder.
We have witnessed a rapid evolution in the air industry as both technology and service have kept pace with the travellers' demands. In the face of increased competition, it is absolutely essential that Air Canada have new capital to develop new routes and to provide new services. It needs to maintain a modern air fleet so that it can continue to serve Canadians proudly around the world. Public participation is essential for
a competitive, financially independent Air Canada, and a strong Air Canada is essential to Canada's competitive airline industry.
For the better part of this century, Canadians have relied upon air travel to span our great distances, open our remote areas and draw us all together as a nation. From its modest beginnings in 1937 Air Canada has grown to play an integral role in our nation building of this great Canada. Air Canada represents a network that has brought us closer together. It represents a network that has linked us with the larger global world, and Canadians are now looking forward to the day when they can share in the direct ownership of this great national enterprise.
Air Canada is a great national institution. I am proud to support this legislation that will allow us to participate in it, just as I am proud of the achievements of a Government that has made air travel safer, more reliable and more accessible for all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I want first to congratulate my colleague on his very fine speech on the need for this legislation.
George Orwell once defined "Doublespeak" as the ability to hold and express two conflicting points of view at the same time. I want to read for the benefit of my colleagues some comments made on Thursday, May 10, 1984, by the then Minister of Transport, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy). He said:
-and 1 myself embarked on a series of personal discussions in Canada and the United States... There were times I had to take issue with those who predicted mass chaos in industry if we attempted reform.
Airline crashes, labour disputes, airline bankruptcies, loss of small community services, all of these were blamed on change, which I would say were properly and effectively disputed and debunked during the course of the hearings.
He went on to explain his view of policy:
The essence of this policy is less regulation and more competition. It is a significant departure from the status quo and reflects the first comprehensive reform of Canadian air policy. It demonstrates the government's confidence in the maturity of Canada's airline industry to respond to the challenges of increased competition.
This policy discards the concept that the airline industry is a public utility. Instead, it introduces the idea that commercial competition is the basis of a healthy air transport system.
It seems to me that the then Minister of Transport, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry, was an eloquent speaker for the privatization of Air Canada. I wonder if my hon. colleague from St. Catharines might have a comment about how the Hon. Member has perfected "Doublespeak" so that he can now oppose what he so fervently supported only a brief time ago.

Mr. Speaker, it has been said of Canadians that we are a pragmatic lot. There is a tremendous difference between 1937 and 1987. There has been a growth in the
June 7, 1988

airlines and in the maturity of this nation. Air Canada has matured as an airline. My friend from Winnipeg-Fort Garry noted that change, and was in a position to do something about it. That was what he was doing, but he did not go far enough.
It became the opportunity of this Government, particularly the Deputy Prime Minister, who in 1979 indicated that safety would always be a priority concern of any Government to which he belonged and that transportation should be governed by the economic sector with a great role being played by the private sector.
A member of the Opposition who once held an important role sees the issue differently today. However, in 1988, the role of Air Canada can only be one in which it is given an opportunity to compete with other airlines without the regulations that encumbered the Air Canada of yesterday. That is what we are doing with this Bill.

Mr. Speaker, on the assumption that my hon. friend from St. Catharines is a good free enterpriser who is in favour of competition and private investment, I would assume as well that he believes that the investors in any profitable corporation should have an opportunity to make a return on those investments in the form of dividends, interest or both.
Why should Canadians or employees of Air Canada who are also Canadians buy shares in a company that had a $45-million net profit last year after taxes but paid no dividends? In 1986, it had a $40-million profit but paid no dividends. Does the Hon. Member think that that is proper? Do the taxpayers of Canada not have just as much right for an opportunity for return on their investment as any single private investor?

Mr. Speaker, I can only ask my hon. friend to wait until 1990 to see what kind of dividend Air Canada will then pay. I recall that that question was raised by the Hon. Member himself at the Standing Committee on Transport. It was pointed out then that the Government of Canada did receive some return for the great service of Air Canada, but the point to be made now is that, yes, as a free enterpriser I agree that the people of Canada should be able to share in the growth and the wealth of an industry whose role is expanding and enlarging. We asked the employees themselves if they wanted to share in this, and of course they do. They want to be part of this growth. They want to be able to share in the profit of their labours. This is the opportunity we are giving them and the people of Canada. We are giving them an opportunity to share in that growth that is bound to take place in the future, just as it has in the past.

Mr. Speaker, we intend to oppose the privatization of Air Canada today as we have on earlier occasions and as we will at every stage at which this Bill is discussed. We do that because we see this proposal being made not because there is any real economic or financial justification for the idea but simply because it is part of the
Air Canada
ideological baggage the Conservative Government carries with it. It is part of its belief that anything the private sector does is better and more efficient than what can be done by publicly-owned companies.
The facts and the record of Air Canada prove that to be completely false. After all, let us recall that Air Canada was established as a Crown corporation by a Liberal Government generations ago because the then Government and the people of Canada realized that an airline which flew regularly from the Atlantic to the Pacific was necessary for Canada and because the private investors were not interested in such an airline. They could not see that they would make a profit in the early years. Therefore, Air Canada was established.
Air Canada has been an efficient company. It has provided service and it is rated internationally as one of the best, most efficient airline companies in the world. It has been well managed and it has been efficient. It has provided service to most parts of Canada, not just to the major cities. To the best of its ability, it has met the needs of the Canadian people.
We are told that part of the reason for privatizing Air Canada is that Air Canada needs new aeroplanes, which it does, and that these new aeroplanes, needed to replace the aging aeroplanes it is now using, will cost billions of dollars. The sale of shares the Government is proposing will only bring in $300 million.
Analysts in the business of watching how money is raised have indicated that there are other ways to raise money. The Government could permit Air Canada to borrow the money. After all, that would not add to the real debt of Canada because Air Canada has been sufficiently profitable to pay the interest and eventually repay the loans.

The Canadian public supports the belief that Air Canada should remain public. Two polls done earlier this year, one by Gallup and one by Environics, show that by a two-to-one majority people believe that Air Canada should not be privatized. Economists in the business world, business analysts, and the head of British Air, all of whom believe in privatization, have said that partial privatization is a mistake, that partial privatization will not work.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: They want the whole thing. Do you agree with them?
Mr. Speaker, I guess the polls showing how low the Conservative Party is in public opinion-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: Come on down and run against me.

Mr. Speaker, I am quite prepared to listen to the Hon. Member for Brampton-Georgetown (Mr. McDermid) make his own speech, and I will not interrupt. However, if he is going to interrupt me I want to deal with his interruptions. The reason he is so nervous and so busy interrupting,

June 7, 1988
Air Canada
interjecting, and shouting, is that he knows he is not going to be here after the next election.
Ele asks me whether I agree with the people who are saying that the company should be 100 per cent privatized. I do not agree with them but they are saying, and I wish he would listen, that either the company should remain as a Crown corporation or it should be 100 per cent privatized. The Government does not have the guts to propose 100 per cent privatization because it knows the public is opposed to that. The Government has opened the door to 100 per cent privatization by bringing forth this proposal for partial privatization.
Those who believe in 100 per cent privatization say that partial privatization is a mistake and will not work. It will not work because there is a requirement in this Bill that the company retain its bilingual status. That is going to cost the company money. It requires that the head office remain in Montreal. That may not be the best business decision. It requires that the maintenance bases in Winnipeg, Montreal, and Toronto be maintained. They say that that is not necessarily a good business decision. They say that we ought to go for 100 per cent privatization, which this Bill does not provide for.
I want to raise several other points which have not been dealt with. We are told that the Government wants to privatize because the private company will be able to operate much more efficiently because of deregulation. We copied our deregulation system from the United States. We now know that many of the people, groups, and organizations in the United States which believed that deregulation would bring benefits in the United States, having now had the experience of a number of years of deregulation, realize that deregulation in the United States was a mistake. We ought to learn from that.
For example, in a June 1988 issue of Consumer Reports magazine issued in the United States the serious problems facing the United States as a result of their 1978 deregulation policy are discussed. This is the same situation which a privatized Air Canada will face following deregulation in Canada which was begun by the then Minister of Transport in the Liberal Government, the Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy), and continued by the present Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) under the Conservative Government.
I want to put on the record the views of the American Consumers' Association because the Canadian Consumers' Association has been one of the biggest supporters of deregulation. The article reads in part as follows:
We recently surveyed more than 400 Consumer Reports readers who are fliers. Nearly half said that air travel is generally worse today than it was 10 years ago, before deregulation. Less than 20 percent said it was generally better. When we asked recent fliers if they had any specific complaints about their latest flight, we got an outpouring of grievances. Almost half reported their flight departed more than 15 minutes late; nearly one in five said it was more than an hour late. Half the readers called the seating "very crowded,"-
-anyone who has travelled on our planes recently knows how crowded they can be-
-and one-third said their food was "unappetizing."
That certainly sounds familiar.
They reported long lines at check-in (28 percent), overbooked planes (14 percent), and an unacceptably long wait for baggage (19 percent).
All this is a far cry from what was expected from deregulation. Deregulation held out to consumers the promise of low fares, better service, more competition, and a boom in travel.
That is just what we heard a few moment ago from the Member for St. Catharines (Mr. Reid). The article goes on:
Last year, names like Air Atlanta, Air South, Chicago Air, Gulf Air, McClain, Royale Airlines, Royal West, and TranStar vanished from terminals in airports around the nation. They join a raft of other more familiar names like Republic, Western, USA ... All of them have been merged, purged, or submerged, leaving behind an industry of eight major airlines, each enjoying local monopolies or shared monopolies, and each serviced by smaller commuter lines that have affiliations with one or more of the giants.
Well, Mr. Speaker, is that not precisely what has happened here? Have we not, despite deregulation, the situation of having two and a half giants; Air Canada and Canadian International, and, to a lesser extent but coming up quickly, Wardair? This is what has happened. The article continues:
Airfares, which dropped sharply because of aggressive competition from upstart airlines, have already started to rise-
That is in the United States and we are going to see that happen in Canada as well. The article continues:
"You ain't seen nothin' yet," says Julius Maldutis, vice president for aviation research at Salomon Brothers, Inc. He predicts that cheaper fares will be further encumbered by onerous restrictions. "You'll still have discount fares, but the availability will be restricted," he says.
I could continue to quote from that article but I think I have said enough to indicate what has happened in the United States and what is going to happen in Canada as deregulation continues to bite further and further.
There are other problems involved. We have heard strong rumours that Air Canada vice-presidents are already strongly lobbying the Government to remove the bilingualism guarantees in the legislation. Members from Quebec should be worried, particularly Members from Montreal, because we know that the main centre for travellers is not Montreal but Toronto. We had a bitter experience in Winnipeg. When Air Canada began, its head office was located in Winnipeg, along with the major maintenance base. When Air Canada officials decided that its operations should be in Montreal, they did not explain to the Government that they had legitimate reasons for moving its head office, maintenance base and other facilities from Winnipeg to Montreal. Instead, they moved in stages, first with the headquarters, then other facilities, and finally the maintenance base.
The Member for Selkirk-Interlake (Mr. Holtmann) is not so old that he cannot remember the pain and unanimous hostility felt not only by the unions and workers involved but by the business community over this move and how Winnipeg was shafted.
June 7, 1988

I suggest to Members of Parliament from Montreal that they keep a very careful eye on Air Canada when it is privatized. I will not be surprised if Air Canada facilities, now mainly centered in Montreal, are eventually moved quietly and surreptitiously to Toronto. Members may suggest that the Bill does not permit this, but we know from experience how a company can get around promises and legislation when it is interested in making a profit.
There is no provision to ensure that when the privatized company purchases new aircraft part of the production of the new planes will be done in Canada. According to my information, until now the wings for McDonnell Douglas aircraft that have been purchased by Air Canada were produced in Toronto. I also believe that some of the work done on other planes was carried out by Canadair in Montreal.
We know that the Post Office, in its determination to make a profit, has taken the contract to move mail originating in Canada to destinations in Europe away from Canadian air carriers and given it to a United States firm. I am sure that this contract formed a substantial part of the business of Air Canada and Canadian International Airlines.
The Post Office was given a directive by the Government to be as financially efficient as possible. Naturally, if it can get a better deal from a European carrier it will do so, ignoring the fact that it may lead to job loss in Canada.
Air Canada is looking at the purchase of new airplanes from Airbus. One must question whether any part of the Airbus aircraft will be built in Canada since it has no facilities here. Furthermore, if the purpose of privatization is to make a company as financially efficient as possible, why would it not buy airplanes as cheaply as possible unless otherwise directed by the Government?
Some government Members will suggest that the privatization still leaves the Government of Canada with a majority share of the company. However, the Government has already said that its share will be operated in a passive way, meaning that the private owners will make the decisions, including the decision to buy as cheaply as possible.
I ask Members from Toronto, Montreal and Winnipeg, where there are sizeable aircraft industries employing thousands of people, what will be the effect on those cities, those workers and on the business community if Air Canada is permitted to buy aircraft from Airbus in Europe or anywhere else, simply because they are cheaper? We believe it is important to take into account the adverse effects of such a decision.
The privatization of Air Canada will mean that it will be primarily concerned with the major centres of Toronto, Vancouver and Montreal, where the most money will be made. We are opposed to that kind of division in Canada. It will result in three groups of Canadians, with Canadians living in the major cities getting first class service, those living in other centres like Calgary, Regina, Winnipeg and Halifax getting
Air Canada
second class service, while those in rural communities and in the North will get the worst service. That will be the inevitable result of the privatization of Air Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I want to comment on the ramblings on of the Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) who quite clearly substantially lacks knowledge of the airline industry, despite the fact that he has been around this place for quite some time.
He flies every week, like me, and we see each other from time to time. The NDP purport to be the only Party that represents union people. Has he asked whether they are really in favour of it?
I have discussed this with many stewardesses and pilots. The Hon. Member held up a piece of paper, citing it as a poll saying that up to a three-to-one majority of people in Canada oppose what the Government is doing. I defy the Hon. Member to pull out the exact poll and tell us when it was conducted. He should present more substantial statements. I also have a poll that I would like to draw to the attention of the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow). It was published in the Financial Times and it was conducted by Decima. I suppose it is just as valid a poll as the one presented by the Hon. Member. On June 6, 1988, not very long ago, Canadians were asked: The federal Government recently announced that it will reduce its ownership in Air Canada, shares will be sold to Air Canada employees and Canadian investors first, and there will be limits on how many shares any one investor can have and how many of these shares can be owned by foreign investors. What is your view?
I hope the Hon. Member listens to the response, which was that 11 per cent were strongly supportive of this plan, 58 per cent supported it, 21 per cent opposed it, 7 per cent strongly opposed it, and 3 per cent did not know. That is hardly a two to one opposition to what the Government has done.
The next question asked was: How do you think this plan will affect the airline's ability to compete and grow? That is a fair question and it was asked of Canadians who, the Hon. Member purports, do not support this. Eight per cent said it will have a very positive effect, 64 per cent said it would have a positive effect, 20 per cent said it would have a negative effect, and 4 per cent said it would have a very negative effect. Do those figures back up the Hon. Member's statement that all Canadians believe that this is going to be very harmful to the industry?
I will read another question: How do you think it will affect the quality of service the airline offers to Canadian travellers? Nine per cent said it would have a positive effect, 65 per cent said it would have a very positive effect, 19 per cent said it would have a negative effect, and 4 per cent said it would have a very negative effect.
COMMONS DEBATES ___________________June 7, 1988
Air Canada
The Hon. Member threw some figures out in this House which distort what really is the case. This particular Decima poll indicates that basically 65 per cent of Canadians support the sale of Air Canada to the private sector. So the Hon. Member's argument requires perhaps some explanation.
The Hon. Member talked about deregulation. This has nothing to do with deregulation, so why bring the subject up? Does he mean that airlines should not continue to be regulated? We have private airlines right now. Are they not under the regulations that exist? Of course, they are. That is a different issue.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ken James (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have the opportunity today to speak on this very important Bill allowing for the participation of the Canadian public in the ownership of Air Canada. I would like to list some reasons why interest in participation and purchase has received such strong support from so many sources in Canada.
My colleagues, both on the government side and opposite, were talking about public reaction to the sale of Air Canada. The polling conducted by the Financial Times and Decima was mentioned. I would like to discuss the area of service and what is important in servicing Canadians. Air Canada has a long tradition of service and it is important that we mention that aspect. In a poll in relation to service the question was asked: "How do you think it will affect the quality of service that the airline offers to Canadian travellers?" It is noted that 74 per cent of those polled had a very positive reaction that it would maintain and enhance the type of service that Canadians are looking for from Air Canada. We should take heed of that.
It is also important that all Members have the opportunity of noting what was stated by Mr. Ed Godin, a spokesman for the pilots. As we all know, pilots have been very positive about the sale of Air Canada for a good number of years. The Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) noted earlier that he thought a number of employees were against the sale. Mr. Godin, when speaking about the other unions, stated: "We find their Members don't share the opinions of their union leaders", and that the union leaders are speaking out. That is quite common and it concerns me that the leadership do not take a plebiscite of their members or present to them the pluses and minuses of being able to purchase stock in Air Canada. They simply go out and make a statement. The same thing happens in my riding of Sarnia-Lambton in connection with free trade. There have been instances where leaders of unions have campaigned against the free trade initiative, whereas probably in the area of 80 per cent of the unionized members are very positive and understand the positive aspects that the free trade initiative will carry forth.
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I wonder if the Hon. Member could advise when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) will take a poll of the Canadian people on trade issues?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Hon. Parliamentary Secretary may resume on debate.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
speechtext:
I am not sure, Mr. Speaker, what type of point of order that was, but it was an interjection from my colleague opposite.
Air Canada
In addressing that very point, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Government were elected to lead and show leadership in this country and maintain good government. Certainly, within that mandate international trade conditions have to be assessed. We would be a sorry lot if we did not adjust to the changing times and take into consideration having a treaty with our most important customer.
When talking about the union leaders Mr. Godin stated: "We find their members don't share the opinions of the union leaders. There's an effort within the unions to counter some of the statements of the union leaders". Mr. Godin further stated: "One flight attendant in Toronto has complained that her union is wasting its money to fight the deal while the pilots are using their money to get a good deal". The pilots are putting it in the sock in order to save it and have a good deal! I thought that was a very interesting quote.
The legislation responds to the changing needs of Air Canada within an economically deregulated air transport industry. This Government has paved the way for that to be done, which is very good for the industry. It provides the freedom and flexibility that will enable Air Canada to meet the challenges of a competitive and global environment. The legislation provides for the orderly transition of Air Canada, as a mature and responsive Canadian company, from a Crown corporation to a publicly held Canadian corporation. It will enable Air Canada to build upon the high level of performance it has demonstrated over its 51 year history. It will support the high level of personal identification that Canadians have and feel for Air Canada as our national flag carrier. We all know there is a very strong feeling in Canada about Air Canada, and certainly among many people who never board an airplane.
They feel positive about the Air Canada name and the airline. It is important that that be maintained, and it certainly will be. It has had a long and illustrious experience in Canada of handling the travelling public. When looking at the polls, it is important to note that a number of people who do not travel, unlike most Members in the House, have perhaps an even more positive feeling about Air Canada.
A few years ago, Air Canada was our only national airline. Today, we have Canadian Airlines International and its partners challenging Air Canada and its partners in national and regional markets across the country. In my riding of Sarnia-Lambton we have Air Ontario, a partner of Air Canada. It is a regional airline. Five months ago Canadian partners started to fly out of Sarnia on a regular basis. Therefore, we have excellent service in a metro area of approximately 87,000 people, and a county city, urban area of approximately 120,000. Air Ontario provides an excellent and competitive service. If one flies out at 7 a.m. to Toronto and connects with Air Canada one can be in Ottawa by 9.15 a.m. The same applies to Canadian Airlines International. It flies out of Sarnia at 7.05 a.m. That example in my own area illustrates the type of service provided to the smaller urban areas in Canada.

June 7, 1988
Air Canada
Wardair is also competing with the two major domestic air carriers in the domestic areas as well as in the charter business. That adds another dimension to the domestic airline business and its competitiveness. The other day I had to have my flight changed and it was changed over to Wardair. That other dimension adds competition, which makes for good service.
One might mention Wardair and the type of private sector competitiveness that Air Canada was experiencing. I note here that in September, 1987, Wardair successfully raised $125 million in a public equity issue to buy more airplanes. That illustrates the competitiveness that Air Canada was experiencing from the private sector where companies could go out and raise moneys, whereas Air Canada was not in the position to do so.
The changes that have been brought about by increased competition in the airline industry have taken place as a result of economic regulatory reform that has been brought on by the Government. This has led to competition for consumer dollars which, in turn, has resulted in lower fares. It is important to the service of Canadians that we have competition and lower fares. Americans have expressed to me their amazement with respect to the fares that we pay to go from one part of Canada to another. We are also interested in increased service and the growth of many smaller airlines serving regional needs.
I found it interesting to read an article which appeared recently in the the Winnipeg Free Press written by Dian Cohen who stated:
The fundamental facts are these. Air Canada, as a creature of the federal government, is dependent on the government for its capital requirements. Air Canada operates as best it can as a private sector participant, in that it must endeavour to balance the books and make a profit. But it does not have the ability, as other private sector companies have, of going into the market place to invite equity participation when it needs a cash infusion.
She went on to state:
Air Canada desperately needs a cash infusion right now-it has made a few million dollars in profits in the past couple of years, but nowhere near the $350 million to $1 billion it needs to replace its aging fleet with newer, quieter and more comfortable airplanes.
It has to replace those planes. Who will do it? Will the federal Government come up with the money? It is for more than competitive reasons that the fleet has constantly been renewed. Planes have geriatric problems just as people do.
She goes on to deal with certain jets with which Air Canada has had problems. The author of this article is a reputable economist. She deals with the options that are available:
Option number one-that the Government will simply give Air Canada the money-is possible. It will mean, since the government of Canada is still spending about $25 billion more each year than it takes in in revenue that either taxes will have to go up, or the government will have to put Air Canada's needs above the needs of farmers, the oil patch, the unemployed, day care-
In order to come up with this amount of money something has to be sacrificed. That is of great concern to me, as it should be to everyone in the House.
In a recent article in the Vancouver Province of May 24, 1988, it is stated that if the Liberals and the New Democrats intend to do all they can to stymie the sale of shares in Air Canada, they had better spell out loud and clear how they expect the airline to raise the money to replace its aging aircraft.
The article goes on to state that the Liberals and New Democrats have offered no cogent reasons why Air Canada should remain as a Crown corporation, or solutions to its financing problems. "They should either put up or shut up and let the sale of these shares go on".
There are features of Air Canada as a Crown corporation that Canadians have valued in the past. Public participation will ensure that Air Canada does not lose sight of the values, and nor will public participation in any way detract from the high level of service Canadians have come to expect from Air Canada. The airline will continue its alliances with regional air carriers, which will provide air service to passengers from smaller centres. In a competitive market it makes sound commercial sense for Air Canada to maintain and improve upon joint scheduling with its regional carriers.
The airlines will still be working together to improve the industry generally. We believe Air Canada will continue to pursue opportunities to develop alliances and partnerships and to meet consumer demand. That is what the free enterprise spirit is all about.
In fact, Air Canada's commercial strategy has always been built upon good service and good value to customers. The interests of Air Canada's new shareholders will go hand in hand with those of the consumers. If Air Canada continues to provide good service and good value, it will continue to attract customers and will provide returns for the shareholders. When employees work for a company and are anxious to buy shares in the company they know the real potential of the company and are anxious to participate.
In the past few weeks I have heard criticism of the proposal to open Air Canada to public participation. It has been argued that Air Canada must remain a Crown corporation in order to serve a public policy role. What is the public policy role that Air Canada serves?
All airlines serve an important public service, providing access to regional, national and international destinations in a safe way, conveniently. We want it to be economical. Are Air Canada's routes and passengers more valuable than those of, say, Canadian Airlines? I believe not. It is very important that we have a deregulated and competitive situation.
Crown ownership of Air Canada is not required to ensure this service. What is required is healthy and open competition, exactly what this legislation will provide.
June 7, 1988

One major area of concern that does fall within the realm of public policy is the safety of the travelling public. Our Government has paid a lot of attention to safety issues in the airline industry. The Aeronautics Act of 1985 laid the foundation for a good, solid, regulatory framework. We have excellent enforcement by Transport Canada.
It is important that Canadians understand that when the Government came into office and took over the management of the company and was looking at privatization we developed some very sound ground rules. I have stated them a number of times before when I was very involved with legislation concerning Canadair, Teleglobe and de Havilland. There was a very sound basis for us to evaluate whether privatization should take place. Certainly, changing economic environment must be considered. We must look at effectiveness. There is abundant evidence to suggest that many Crown corporations are not as effective in serving their clients as the private sector can be. We must take that into consideration as we evaluate. Public ownership of Crown corporations places enormous demands on the Government. We have spoken about this a great deal today. Public institutions use taxpayers' money to operate. At times having Government involved even though just at arm's length tends to inhibit good, sound operation of companies. These facts were all taken into consideration when the Government moved into privatizing 13 different concerns.
I appreciate the opportunity to speak to this important legislation to explain why the Government moved toward its important decision on Air Canada. We are proud of Air Canada's achievement. As a member of the Government I am proud of this legislation that will enable Air Canada to grow and enable individual Canadians to share in its prosperity, its service to the country and to all Canadians.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I regret the fact that we are down to ten minutes, but I will do what I can to highlight my major concerns about the privatization of Air Canada, which is the purpose of Bill C-129.
Mr. Speaker, I will be perfectly frank: I am against the Government's Bill. I am against the Tories' proposal for privatization, and I think the mechanism to bring this about was designed in haste and that the Government has given no serious consideration to the impact of its decision on the industry and Air Canada itself.
In this case, Mr. Speaker, we have a proposal for privatization that was drafted, as I said earlier, in haste, and which I think is surprisingly ill-prepared. Of course, we are used to that in the House by now. The Government always seems to be rushing in its legislation, and it is unable to manage the time of the House effectively.
Mr. Speaker, the Government decided to privatize Air Canada because the Corporation has to buy new aircraft. It needs a capital injection of about $300 million to renew its fleet. As we said earlier, these requirements are not new. In years gone by, the Corporation has been able to buy the replacement aircraft it needs, and I think it will still be able to do so if it remains in the public sector.
The Government tells us it is going to give Air Canada back to Canadians by letting them purchase shares in the company. Mr. Speaker, Air Canada already belongs to Canadians. It is a public corporation, a Crown corporation, 100 per cent owned by Canadians. What this Government is about to do is sell us something we already own. This isn't very logical, but that's Tory logic for you. We will make more money by investing in a company that no longer belongs to us. The purpose of Bill C-129 is to take Air Canada away from us. It's like selling the furniture to buy the House. It's like giving the lease to strangers, whose interests may be very different from the needs and interests of Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, privatizing Air Canada does not make sense. We don't have to sell the pride and joy of Canadians that happens to be making a profit. In fact, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said during the last election campaign, and I repeat it here today: "Canada needs a national airline", said Mr. Mulroney, and "I agree that Canada must keep this national airline".
Mr. Speaker, I agree with the Prime Minister. With a lot of time and effort, energy and skill and capital investment, we

June 7, 1988
Air Canada
here in Canada have made Air Canada a going concern with an international reputation. Now the Government is getting ready to dismantle all that because the company needs airplanes.
Mr. Speaker, because I am short of time, in the few minutes available to us, I would like to touch on a most important subject related to my work as official languages critic, namely, clause 10 of Bill C-129, which reads, "The Official Languages Act applies to the Corporation."
In the few moments at my disposal, I would share with the House my concerns on this obligation, this provision of the Bill.
Mr. Speaker, as a federal institution, Air Canada has always been subject to the Official Languages Act since 1969. In an appearance before the Official Languages Committee on April 15, 1987, Mr. Pierre Jeanniot, President and Chief Executive Officer of Air Canada, said:
Air Canada, through its people, extends the reality of a bilingual Canada to every place we serve. I believe that these examples, only a few of many, also effectively demonstrate that bilingualism does work in a commercial environment. It takes a lot of effort and dedication and commitment, but it can and it is being accomplished.
Since the subject of privatization has been raised, increasing pressure has come from the company, which feels that clause 10 of Bill C-129 will put too heavy a burden on it compared to its competitors. I know that because I have met company representatives who told me of their fears. They raised a number of issues, including services provided by a third party; Bill C-72, the new Official Languages Act I hope will soon be passed by this House, and how it will apply; bilingual signage; supplementary audits by the Commissioner of Official Languages, Treasury Board and the Department of the Secretary of State; the possibility of court challenges; language of work, both with respect to documentation and computer systems; and the role of supervisors. The corporation is also concerned about the primacy of the Official Languages Act over the Aeronautics Act and the National Transportation Act, problems with personnel logistics and the interpretation of "significant demand", and finally, potential conflicts with provincial legislation such as Bill 101 in Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, I have discussed all these concerns with corporation representatives for some time. To hear these people talk, you would think they were headed for certain financial disaster if they ever had to comply with the Official Languages Act!
I listened very carefully to these people and I understand their concerns. Although I could take their fears one by one and put them to rest, I don't think this is either the time or the place to do so. However, one argument I utterly refuse to accept. According some Air Canada representatives, there is no way they can live with Bill C-72 in a commercial, profit-oriented environment. In this respect, Mr. Speaker, I am supported and by the President of Air Canada himself, Mr. Pierre Jeanniot, who told the Committee about a year ago, and I quote:
In pragmatic terms, while our commitment is derived from a strong social belief in the equality of both languages and equal opportunities for all Canadians, we have also determined that bilingualism makes good commercial sense.
Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that this statement makes eminent sense. In the case of Air Canada and Bill C-129, I think there is room for adjustments, for specific arrangements to accommodate the company which, I agree, operates in a very particular and very competitive environment. The Official Opposition intends to propose such arrangements when the Bill is considered in Committee.
However, although we are open to adjustments, these should not be allowed to alter the basic principle. Canadians need a national carrier, but they also need a carrier that, partly privatized or not, respects the basic characteristics of this country, and I am referring to the English-French linguistic duality, a carrier that is able to offer services at all times in either official language of this country, from Vancouver to Halifax, from Yellowknife to Chicoutimi. This is a sacred principle that must not be altered, with or without privatization.
Mr. Speaker, I raised this point because I think it is extremely important. I would like to see the Government maintain what Bill C-129 contains with respect to official languages. I don't want to see the Government's commitment watered down. However I would not want to see Air Canada obliged to work in a competitive climate where it is not playing on a level field. I think we can allay Air Canada's fears about the Official Languages Act and its application to Bill C-129, while maintaining a certain way of doing things here in Canada for corporations that are privatized. In other words, when we privatize a public service, especially in the transportation sector, the corporation that will be privatized-it will be, because the Government has an overwhelming majority and will probably win the vote-but in any case, if it is privatized Mr. Speaker, there must be a commitment that the future company will remain subject to the Official Languages Act and that ways will be found to deal with the problems of being competitive after privatization.
I do not want Air Canada to be forced to do things that might reduce its competitiveness and give it financial difficulties. But I think that if the Government requires a company to do more than another company in the market, this same Government must guarantee that the company will be compensated for the additional services that it must provide. I am thinking, for example, of the three main aspects: language of work, language of service and equitable representation. There is no doubt that if employees are to work in their own language, English or French, throughout the country, Air Canada will have problems, but there are solutions, in Quebec as in Winnipeg. I think that we can reasonably call upon the expertise of the House and Hon. Members to find a solution to
June 7, 1988

this problem of language of work that might cause major problems for Air Canada.
As for language of service, Mr. Speaker, I maintain today that Air Canada has been required to use both for almost 20 years. It has gained some experience. The President and CEO of the company, Mr. Jeanniot, said so in committee. It can be done very easily and with good will if the company just understands that it must serve the Canadian public in both official languages throughout its operations. I think that we already have good experience and some background in this.
I see no problems with equitable representation. It costs the company no more to hire competent people who reflect the country's demographic makeup. As I already said, I think that Air Canada already has some experience with all these questions. It is possible to do so and we must continue, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext:

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-72 to amend the Official Languages Act says that the federal Government should support the language minorities in Canada including the anglophone minority in Quebec. The Meech Accord says that the English community in Quebec is part of the fundamental character of Canada and that the federal and provincial Governments must preserve this fundamental character.
Why then is the Quebec Government now questioning certain provisions of Bill C-72? Bill C-72 is totally consistent with the Meech Accord which Quebec initiated. The Meech Accord does not give priority to Quebec in language matters. Certain language rights were entrenched in the Constitution in 1867 and once again in 1982, and the federal Official Languages Act was enacted in 1970.
The Quebec Government should stop confusing the public on these issues. Language rights in Canada are fundamental and the promotion of one language should never be done at the expense of the other.

Mr. Speaker, on this occasion of Italy Week right here in Ottawa, it is a real pleasure and a great honour for me to respectfully salute all Italian Canadians, who have enriched our Canadian culture with their traditions that are so warm and colorful.
I wish to take this national opportunity to draw particular attention to the multicultural dimension of our wonderful constituency of LaSalle-Emard, which has two very active Italian parishes: Maria Madre Dei Christiani, ably led by Father Duchini, and San Giovanni Di Bosco, whose pastor is Father Piol.
Since we are not allowed to use the language of Dante, so rich as it is, in this House, I will simply use this expression known in all times and civilizations: "Bravo" to all Italian Canadians!

subtopic: APPEAL WON BY ALBERTA SCHOOLTEACHER AGAINST CONVICTION FOR INCITING HATRED
APPEAL WON BY ALBERTA SCHOOLTEACHER AGAINST CONVICTION FOR INCITING HATRED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not easy, in a society committed to freedom of speech, to curb abuse of that freedom. A blow for truth was struck with the conviction, in 1985, of James Keegstra for teaching Alberta high school students about a Jewish conspiracy he thinks is at work in world affairs.
The decision of the Alberta Court of Appeal to quash Keegstra's conviction illustrates the difficulty Canadians face in curbing lies and deceit used for racist purposes. Mr. Justice R. P. Kerans and his two colleagues assert that the Charter of Rights and Freedoms protects such freedom of speech and that the charge of inciting hatred against an identifiable group must be corroborated by evidence of such hatred and those exposed to the incitement.
An appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada regarding this decision is urgently needed. I urge the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) to support the Attorney General of Alberta in obtaining an early hearing by the Supreme Court of Canada.
Canadians want to know what the limits on freedom of speech are in our multicultural society. They need to be assured that incitement to hatred against identifiable groups will not flourish under Charter protection.
June 7, 1988

Mr. Speaker, there is no question that the womb is truly a dangerous place to live. Knowing the current madness prevalent in those who would do away with unborn children, none of us would ever choose to be there today.
The about-to-be-aborted unborn children would agree. Occasionally they do survive the abortion, but who is there to monitor what happens next? Absolutely no one except those who are intent on preventing and destroying life.
As Members of Parliament we must call for and support pro-life legislation. As Members of Parliament we must question whether a woman has a right to terminate her pregnancy by ensuring the death of her child.
As Members of Parliament we must not condone the future destruction of our unborn children by handing them over to the canonized law breaker Elenry Morgantaler, who now views his mandate for nation-wide abortion clinics and schools, to teach other doctors his perfected death skills.
For us to accept wholesale abortion is to put future generations and ourselves in the hands of those who hold a philosophy of death. All arguments in favour of abortion, infanticide, and euthanasia, reveal that the humanitarian ethic wants to restrict the right to live and expand the right to die and to kill.

[ Translation]

Mr. Speaker, last week, I had the pleasure and the honour to go to the riding of Lac-Saint-Jean and I met working men and women who, it so happened, have the same opinion of the Conservative Government as those in my riding of Montreal- Sainte-Marie. I met old people. They too feel the same way as seniors in Montreal-Sainte-Marie. I met families in Lac-Saint-Jean. They too have the same opinion of the Conservative Government as families in Montreal-Sainte-Marie.
Mr. Speaker, the difference, I learned, is that the people of Lac-Saint-Jean ... no senior citizen there will vote for our national "Charlie Brown." And I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that at this moment... Mr. Bouchard was ahead in the race, but now, he is behind and the people of Lac-Saint-Jean will give a lesson to this Conservative Government, which has been incompetent for the past four years.

Mr. Speaker, the proposed headquarters for the federal space agency must be in Ottawa because it would simply be the right thing to do. The federal Departments and foreign embassies with which it will continually liase are here. Thousands of person years in research and development and related scientific activities are within the National Capital Region and should not be disrupted or relocated. National headquarters, as in most other industrialized nations, should be in the National Capital.
In 1985-86, 44.1 per cent of federal government grants for R and D to industry went to Quebec, with only 5.7 per cent to the National Capital Region. Space plan targets for regional spending show Quebec to get 35 per cent and Ontario 35 per cent.
The space industry wants the agency in Ottawa and so do I. It is the logical decision.

Mr. Speaker, the BBC has illuminated the tragedy behind the veil of secrecy designed by the South African Government to hide its torture and abuse of children. In Canada a lost child is often a victim of the criminal or the insane. In South Africa one seeks a missing black child in a government prison where the acts of the criminal and the insane are sanctioned by racist law.
Today three million black people are risking all to protest their continuing oppression. Under the leadership of COSATU and the churches of South Africa, in the face of uncivilized rejection of non violence by their oppressors, they themselves are trying non violent means of expression one more time. But perhaps the question must be asked: can they, or we who claim to be their supporters, really continue to believe that the violent oppressor will ever concede to a non violent plea? Will we instead find Frederick Douglas to be proven right, that we cannot hope to have the rain of freedom without the thunder and lightning of a liberating storm?
June 7, 1988

Mr. Speaker, David Peterson, Ontario's Premier, has bewildering advice for children and high school students. According to a story in the May 21 Globe and Mail, he told 420 young people that Governments are spending millions of dollars on public awareness, advertising, and medical research on the disease AIDS. Mr. Peterson informed them that it is acceptable to have safe sex with the use of condoms.
Mr. Peterson admits that there is no cure for the dreaded AIDS disease that causes suffering, misery, and heartbreak.
In view of the fact that he was speaking to children and youths, it would seem to me that the subject of safe sex could have been mentioned in a husband-wife context. He could have warned that promiscuity and homosexuality are probably the two greatest causes of AIDS. He could have warned them that the best way to play it safe is to wait for marriage, but he didn't.
Young people need better role models. As the Premier of Ontario, he has an obligation and responsibility to give healthy and intelligent answers to important questions.
Is David Peterson's advice the kind we want to give our children? Surely our children, our students, who will become the men and women of tomorrow, deserve better. Bewildering advice indeed!

subtopic: U.S. COAST GUARD'S SEIZURE OF CANADIAN FISHING VESSEL IN LAKE SUPERIOR
U.S. COAST GUARD'S SEIZURE OF CANADIAN FISHING VESSEL IN LAKE SUPERIOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last December 6, the Michigan Department of Natural Resources and the U.S. Coast Guard seized the Canadian fishing boat Last Time in Canadian waters in Lake Superior.
The vessel, owned by Ferroclad Fisheries of Batchawana, was taken to Sault Ste. Marie, Michigan, and had been in the possession of the Michigan Department of Natural Resources ever since. This has resulted in losses of hundreds of thousands of dollars of income to fishermen.
The captain and crew have been charged with a misdemeanour of fishing with an illegal device, a gillnet, which carries a maximum fine of $500. No conviction has been registered yet against the captain and crew. The fishing vessel which is worth some over $500,000 is still held by the State of Michigan.
The seizure of a Canadian fishing vessel in Canadian waters by the U.S. is illegal. I call on the Government of Canada to demand that this vessel be returned to the owners immediately
because it was seized illegally, that the misdemeanour charges against the fishermen be dropped, and that full restitution for the losses to these fishermen be made by the United States Government.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday's announcement by the President of the Treasury Board (Miss Carney) that cruise ships of 250 or more berths would be allowed duty free entry into Canada on a long term basis was welcome news for the British Columbia cruise ship industry.
Certainly the concerns expressed about this issue over the past week from all quarters of the marine and tourism sectors have been listened to sympathetically by our colleagues in Cabinet. Now the work of the interdepartmental task force, which will look at all aspects of federal policy affecting the cruise industry, must be done thoroughly and urgently, particularly with respect to whether or not over the long term any taxes or tariffs should be charged on the goods consumed or sold aboard cruise ships after 1988, for which they have already been exempted.
Perhaps in all the flurry over this issue, someone missed the important announcement by the Minister of State for Tourism (Mr. Valcourt) on May 25 when he unveiled an $80,000 study to examine the potential for expanding the cruise ship industry on the British Columbia coast. This study will look at port requirements, attractions and services for cruise ship passengers, as well as marketing strategies to attract even more customers to the B.C. west coast.

subtopic: TOXIC WASTES-DUMPING BY EUROPE IN AFRICAN COUNTRIES
TOXIC WASTES-DUMPING BY EUROPE IN AFRICAN COUNTRIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, modern industrial society does not know what to do with its garbage. Cities like Vancouver look for a dump site upcoast or in the interior. Large American cities tow their garbage out to sea or try to palm it off on poorer countries. The situation, however, becomes truly alarming when we deal with toxic waste. The experiences of the Love Canal and other dump sites have shown us that burying it is no solution.
We now hear of European countries that want to export the problem of toxic waste to Africa. A number of them plan to develop a toxic waste site in Benin. We read that Italy has dumped 1,200 tonnes of toxic waste in Nigeria and the

June 7, 1988
containers for this toxic waste were so hot they burned the hands of the workers who handled them despite the fact they were wearing rubber gloves.
We need to recognize that we live in one world, a shrinking world. We cannot store poison in one part of it without damaging all of it. We must learn to stop producing toxic waste rather than trying to bury it.

subtopic: CARDINAL VACHON-FIFTIETH ANNIVERSARY IN RELIGIOUS LIFE
CARDINAL VACHON-FIFTIETH ANNIVERSARY IN RELIGIOUS LIFE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the people of Beauce and Quebec, I wish to pay tribute to a native son who is celebrating his fiftieth anniversary as a priest. I am referring to the illustrious prelate, His Eminence Cardinal Louis-Albert Vachon, Archbishop of Quebec.
This man, devoid of any affectation, has made his mark in the Roman Catholic Church. We admire his tireless dedication to his brothers and sisters in Christ. Cardinal Vachon has always believed that the life and dignity of every human being was worthy of respect.
Mr. Speaker, what is truly remarkable about this man is his abiding sense of justice and equity. As the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said: "In our modern society, the role of the priest has become immeasurably more complex, reflecting the rapid changes in our society".
Wherever there is trouble and despair, a priest is there to bring words of consolation and hope. Your Eminence, I wish you a happy fiftieth anniversary, good health and a long life!

Mr. Speaker, there are many important issues facing the people of Central Nova in the next federal election, but none are as fundamentally important as the issues of honesty and credibility. When the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) ran in Central Nova five years ago, he promised jobs, jobs, jobs. He bragged that when it came to government largess in Central Nova, he was going to make Allan J. look like a schoolboy. Well, we all know who the real schoolboy is. It is the Prime Minister.
In August of 1983, when the Prime Minister ran in Central Nova, there were 4,200 people dependent upon unemployment insurance. Today, four years and ten months later, there are over 6,600 people dependent upon unemployment insurance
benefits in this area. In April the unemployment insurance rate in Pictou County was 31 per cent. Where are the jobs?
The Prime Minister has proven to be a schoolboy who does not do his homework. He deserves a detention. Perhaps he should be made to stay after school and write "I will tell the truth" 6,000 times. Better still, since he is failing so badly, maybe he should just drop out altogether.

Mr. Speaker, the western economy is currently facing the strain of a drought. The federal and provincial Governments are prepared to provide whatever assistance is needed to overcome this natural disaster, yet the man-made problem of high interest rates continues to hurt the prairie economy.
Interest rates are now the single highest expense of nonfarm origin faced by farmers. The rise in interest rates has been a major factor contributing to the decline of farm asset values, and what hurts the farmers hurts the whole prairie population.
The Bank of Canada interest rate policy is having a negative impact on new home construction, retail sales, manufacturing, and dampening the spirit of small business. This is all occurring at a time when the western economy is already in a depressed state.
I realize it is important to control inflation, but a policy which concentrates solely on inflation ignores the negative impact that high interest rates can have on important sectors in other regions of the country.
I call on the Bank of Canada to reassess its position.

Mr. Speaker, Canada's legal system has a long way to go before a court trial can be held in which the accused, and only the accused, is placed on trial. Recent trials have demonstrated, all too often, the licence given to unscrupulous defence counsel to place the victim or victims, almost always women and/or children, on trial, rather than the defendant.
The practice of harassment and intimidation of victim witnesses in Canadian court rooms is one that must be stopped. It degrades the quality of justice in Canada, demeans victims,
June 7, 1988

derogates from their human rights, and disgraces the legal profession by turning the courts into a media backdrop and defence counsel into mercenary actors.
If the legal profession cannot rectify this situation by discipline, then we shall have to by legislation. In either case, Canada's justice system must protect victims and witnesses and not expose them to a form of trial in many ways harsher than that which the defendant undergoes.

subtopic: COMPENSATION SOUGHT FOR OYSTER AND QUAHOG HARVESTERS AND SHIPPERS
COMPENSATION SOUGHT FOR OYSTER AND QUAHOG HARVESTERS AND SHIPPERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Members of the House will recall the extreme bungling that surrounded the federal Government's handling of the mussel toxin case. This mismanagement reached its peak on December 11, 1987, and I quote from a press release from that day: "Health and Welfare Minister Jake Epp and Fisheries Minister Thomas Siddon announced today that an alert is in force on all shellfish from Atlantic Canada". Imagine the chaos and confusion created by that statement.
Protecting the safety and health of Canadians must come first, but surely the federal Government has to recognize that its handling of this problem only served to make a bad situation even worse. For instance, the federal Government ordered that oysters and quahogs already harvested and on their way to markets be destroyed. These producers and shippers are still looking for compensation for their products, which were totally free of toxin; no trace whatsoever was found in them either before they were harvested or in shipment.
I now urge the Ministers concerned to approve these funds as soon as possible.

Mr. Gabriel Fontaine (Levis)t Mr. Speaker, the socialist leader has spoken out against nuclear submarines, thus taking the same position as the Liberal Leader. That is their political choice.
But it's a different story when Canada's ambassador to the United Nations and ex-socialist leader of Ontario endorses his former and future boss wholeheartedly.
Whether he is elected or appointed, an NDP'er will always thumb his nose at integrity. He takes the honours and the
Oral Questions
money, the benefits and the floor, but his philosophy never changes.
When dealing with a Member of the NDP, never forget the old French saying: "Donne a manger a un cochon, il va faire sur ton perron".

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ACQUISITION OF NUCLEAR POWERED SUBMARINES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct my questions to the Prime Minister. In the last two or three days we have been greeted with the spectacle of our Ambassador to the United Nations totally contradicting government policy in the areas of nuclear disarmament, foreign aid, and defence. We have had the spectacle of the Minister of International Trade contradicting the Secretary of State for External Affairs about what to do about the Ambassador to the UN. We have had the Minister of Finance contradicting the Minister of Defence as to what the cost of this very expensive program will be. We have had nothing but a series of confusing and contradictory statements from Ministers of the Crown concerning the silly and ludicrous defence program put forward by the Government.
Under those circumstances, is it not time for the Prime Minister to exercise his responsibility and to ask for a basic review of a program which not only threatens to bankrupt the defence treasury, but also undermines Canada's commitment to the non-proliferation treaty and the commitment we have had to verification and nuclear disarmament?
Is it not time that the Prime Minister stepped into this mess and cleared it up?

subsubtopic: PROPOSED ACQUISITION OF NUCLEAR POWERED SUBMARINES
